title: Stakeholders and their objectives
notes: Authored 2026-10-06 under standard v0.2.0-draft. All claims are provenance generated_gap, verification unverified.

blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Define stakeholders, sort the main internal and external groups apart, state the objectives that different stakeholder groups are likely to hold, and explain how these objectives come into conflict, with examples.

blocks.heading: Stakeholders
blocks.text: A stakeholder is any person or group with an interest in what a business does - anyone affected by its decisions, for better or worse. A lodge's stakeholders include its owners, its staff, the guests, the vegetable supplier, the bank that lent it money, the government that taxes it and the village that lives beside it. The word covers groups inside and outside the business, which is where the internal and external split begins.

blocks.heading: Internal and external stakeholders
blocks.text:
Internal stakeholders are the people inside the business: its workers, its managers and its owners. External stakeholders are everyone with an interest from outside: customers, suppliers, lenders such as banks, the government and the wider community. The boundary is employment and ownership. A driver at a Windhoek courier firm is internal because the firm employs him; a regular customer is external because her link is a purchase, not a job. Owners are internal even when they never visit, because the business is theirs.

One caution: "internal" does not mean "more important". Both sides can decide a business's fate - workers can quit, customers can leave - so a manager has to weigh them all.

blocks.heading: What internal stakeholders want
blocks.text: Each internal group holds objectives that follow from its own position. Workers want fair pay, safe conditions, job security and work that is not unbearable - their interest is the living the business provides. Managers add objectives of their own: a rising career, a salary tied to results, and the standing that comes from running a growing department. Owners want the return on the money they put in: profit, and growth in what the business is worth. When the business does well, these aims usually move together; when it does badly, they pull apart, which is where conflict begins.

blocks.heading: What external stakeholders want
blocks.text: External groups want outcomes that match their own interest. Customers want quality, fair prices and reliable supply. Suppliers want a customer who pays on time and orders again. Lenders want the loan repaid with interest - a bank is likely to watch a business closely once its profits shrink, because the bank's money is at risk in it. Government wants the taxes, the jobs and the legal behaviour the country runs on. The community wants the jobs and the spending a business brings without the noise, the traffic or the pollution. A German carmaker felt the weight of that last objective when a town's objections to its test-track plans forced a redesign: neighbours are stakeholders too, and their objectives can hold up a project for years.

blocks.heading: One decision, many stakeholder effects
blocks.text:
Most decisions a business makes help some stakeholders and work against others. Take a lodge that raises its room prices by 15 per cent.

The owner gains: revenue per room rises, which supports her profit objective. Guests pay more for the same stay, which works against their objective of value, and some may book elsewhere. Workers neither gain nor lose directly, but if the rise drives guests away and the lodge runs short of work, their security is threatened later. The village that sells crafts to guests gains if wealthier visitors spend more.

The manager cannot make the decision "good for stakeholders" in general; she has to judge which groups the business most depends on - and that judgement is what makes stakeholder conflict a live question rather than a definition.

blocks.heading: A wage claim at Tulonga
blocks.text:
Tulonga Farm Supplies in Grootfontein made a profit of N$150 000 last year. Its 25 workers have asked for a 10 per cent wage rise, which would add about N$108 000 to yearly costs.

The workers' objective is fair pay, and the rise is small next to the whole wage bill. The owners' objective is profit, and N$108 000 is most of the N$150 000 they earned, so the two objectives cannot both be fully met. This is a stakeholder conflict: the objectives of the workers and the owners clash over one decision.

settlement exists - a staged rise of 5 per cent now and a further 5 per cent if sales grow, for example - because the objectives of the workers and the owners are not strictly incompatible. What no settlement can do is satisfy both groups in full this year; the owners pay, the workers wait, or both meet in the middle.

blocks.heading: Weighing and compromise
blocks.text: When stakeholder objectives conflict, the business has to weigh them. The usual starting points are: which groups can hurt the business most if they withdraw - workers who strike, customers who leave, a lender who calls in a loan; which objectives the law protects, such as a minimum wage; and how long each group can be kept waiting. Compromise is the normal result: a rise smaller than demanded, a price increase with a loyalty discount for regulars, a cut in hours instead of jobs. The judgement does not end, because the next decision starts the weighing again.

blocks.heading: Whose benefit?
blocks.text: Answers about stakeholder effects often say "this benefits the business" - but a business is not a person, and the phrase hides who gains. Profit goes to owners; a bigger wage bill goes to workers; lower prices go to customers. The discipline is to name the group: "the price rise helps the owners' profit objective but works against customers' objective of low cost" says something that can be checked against each group, while "it is good for the business" leaves the beneficiary unnamed.
